localBiteReport: The most current reports available (with the freshest dated post from July 31, 2026) indicate that August is shaping up as a productive inshore month on Choctawhatchee Bay. Speckled trout, redfish, black drum, and flounder are all listed as active bay targets, with guides working grass flats, oyster beds, docks, bridges, and bayous — especially during early-morning topwater windows before the heat of the day sets in at current water temps of 86°F. A recent angler report out of Santa Rosa Beach noted good numbers of speckled trout along with a notable 40¼-inch, 26-lb bull redfish, consistent with FishingBooker's seasonal summary that bull reds and trophy-sized trout are drawing anglers to the bay right now. Live bait (shrimp, pinfish, mullet) is reported as the most productive approach, though soft plastics and topwater lures are also producing when conditions allow. Note: the most recent dated blog post is from July 31, 2026; individual angler feed entries on captainexperiences.com appear more recent but carry no explicit calendar dates.

aiSummary: August is delivering a productive inshore bite on Choctawhatchee Bay, with speckled trout, redfish, black drum, and flounder all active across grass flats, oyster bars, docks, and bayous — including a notable 40¼-inch, 26-lb bull redfish reported out of Santa Rosa Beach. Today's conditions stack up well early: calm SSW winds at 0–5 mph, a strong spring-tide push off last night's high, and a waning crescent moon favor focused, aggressive feeding in the first few hours after sunrise. A storm window opens after 1 PM with an 11% chance, so plan to be off the water or tucked into protected bayous by early afternoon as the heat index climbs to 103°F.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings serving as the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. Open water here is fully exposed to weather and chop, making it the first spot to become unfishable when wind picks up.
bridge.todaysCall: The falling tide running toward the 3:36 PM low will be your engine here today — current through the pilings should accelerate through mid-morning and into the early afternoon, pushing bait and concentrating fish on the down-current side. Hit the bridge early, well before the post-1 PM storm window, since this exposed open-water spot is the first to go bad if afternoon weather materializes. Light SSW winds at 0–5 mph keep conditions manageable this morning, so you'll have a clean shot at working the lee-side pilings. Slightly stained water in bright sun favors natural presentations — live shrimp or pinfish tight to the pilings are your best bet, consistent with the bay-wide live-bait trend. Black drum and sheepshead are especially reliable on the structure itself; trout and reds will be holding in the current seam just off the pilings.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the mouth. Oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime holding area, and tree cover keeps the bayou a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and holds bass alongside smaller reds.
alaqua.todaysCall: The spring-tide-driven falling water will be draining Alaqua Bayou steadily through the morning and into early afternoon, pushing baitfish out over the oyster bars at the mouth — station yourself there to intercept reds and trout stacking up on that outgoing flow. The tree canopy will provide meaningful relief on a day where the heat index hits 103°F, making this a comfortable choice for an extended morning session. Light stain and bright overhead sun favor slower, natural presentations, so lean on live shrimp under a cork or a slow-rolled soft plastic near the oyster structure. The protected character of this bayou makes it a safe choice if afternoon clouds begin building early around the post-1 PM storm window. Bay-wide reports confirm reds and trout are both active right now, and Alaqua's documented redfish population makes it one of the stronger bets on the bay today.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange Bayou, which translates to less-educated fish and potentially more willing biters. Interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally appear at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is somewhat less protected than LaGrange when weather builds.
basin.todaysCall: The falling tide through mid-afternoon will be pulling water off Basin Bayou's interior grass flats, concentrating reds in the deeper edges and cuts — get in early and work the skinny water while there's still enough depth to move around. Light winds this morning give you a genuine shot at sight-fishing for tailing reds in less than two feet before the flat drains too shallow, and the lower fishing pressure here means those fish are less likely to have seen a bait recently. Slightly stained water limits pure sight-fishing visibility a bit, so supplement visual hunting with a slow-moving live shrimp or weedless soft plastic that puts scent and vibration in the water. The post-1 PM storm window and this spot's relatively less-protected character mean you'll want to be wrapping up by midday. Pompano at the mouth is less likely given it's now August rather than late spring, so focus your energy on the reds inside.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is consistently regarded as a top trout producer in this area, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats holding redfish year-round. Deep holes inside hold black drum and sheepshead, and the bayou offers the most protected water on the north side of the bay, making it the go-to refuge when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the single strongest call on the bay today — the falling tide will activate the oyster bars at the mouth right through the morning, setting up a classic trout-and-redfish ambush, and the bay-wide report confirms both species are feeding aggressively right now. Work the mouth structure first in the low-light window just after the 6:07 AM sunrise, when topwater and surface-disturbing presentations can be especially effective given the calm winds and spring-tide current. As the sun climbs and the heat index approaches 103°F, push inside to the deeper holes for black drum and sheepshead, or stay on the grass flats for reds. The protected nature of this bayou gives you a comfortable margin if the post-1 PM storm window produces anything — you can ride it out here more safely than at exposed spots like the bridge. Live shrimp is the percentage play in slightly stained water and bright sun.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water with bass and smaller reds. It is short, tucked in, and consistently the safest fishery when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: On a falling tide today, Four Mile Creek will be flushing baitfish and crustaceans toward the mouth — position yourself at or just inside the creek mouth to intercept trout, reds, and flounder stacking up on that outgoing flow. This is one of the bay's most protected spots, so it's an excellent choice if you want to fish late into the morning and still feel safe about the post-1 PM storm window. The short run from Shipyard Marina also means minimal exposure to open-bay chop if afternoon conditions develop. Flounder are a realistic target at the mouth in slightly stained water — a live shrimp or mud minnow on a jig head dragged slowly along the bottom is hard to beat. Reds and trout will be in the bends and grass edges inside the creek; work them with live shrimp or a slow-rolling soft plastic matched to the stained water.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are the peak window, with trout stacking on grass in two to four feet of water, and Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular pressure but produces consistently, though it is further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous — factor in run time.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown is purpose-built for exactly the conditions showing today — calm winds, a spring-tide falling tide, and an early-morning window before the heat index hits 103°F. Get there at or just after sunrise at 6:07 AM and work the grass flats in two to four feet with topwater early, then transition to live shrimp or soft plastics as the sun gets high. The bay-wide bite report specifically references speckled trout as the headliner in this Santa Rosa Beach area, and a recent report noted excellent trout numbers consistent with guides working these same summer grass-flat patterns. Factor in the longer run time from the 331 Bridge area when planning your morning — you want to maximize time on the flat before the bite dies in the midday heat. Be off the open water well before the post-1 PM storm window; the run back adds risk if weather builds.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — this dashboard's top trout producer — means LaGrange's oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water. It is an interior spot with limited documented fishing history, but its small, sheltered character makes it a reasonable calm-water fallback when wind builds on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet Bayou's best argument today is its connection to LaGrange Bayou: the same falling tide draining LaGrange's system will be moving through here, and if fish are stacked on LaGrange's oyster bars, the quieter water of Mallet could hold less-pressured fish following the same pattern. Today's light winds make this a low-priority pick over LaGrange itself — save Mallet for days when you want to escape pressure or probe overlooked water. That said, if you're already working LaGrange and have time, poking into Mallet with a live shrimp or soft plastic along the banks is a low-risk bonus. There's limited documented history here, so treat any activity as a discovery rather than a sure thing. Plan around the post-1 PM storm window regardless — interior bayou or not, you'll want to be sorted before that window opens.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees less pressure due to its distance from main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: If you're willing to make the long run from the 331 Bridge area, Mack Bayou offers the same oyster-bar-and-grass-flat pattern as Alaqua and LaGrange but with meaningfully less fishing pressure — and on a day when those closer bayous may draw crowds, that can matter. The falling tide through the morning will work the oyster structure and grass edges here just as it will elsewhere on the bay; plan to arrive early and work the mouth structure first. Calm winds today make the long open-water run reasonable, but factor in your return trip before the post-1 PM storm window — that's a significant exposure risk on the run back if weather develops. Pair the trip with Hewett and Buck Bayous to the east to make the run worthwhile. Redfish, trout, and flounder are all plausible targets consistent with the bay-wide bite report.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, sharing the same protected-bayou habitat with oyster bars, marsh grass, and a few deeper interior holes. It is another long-run destination from the 331 Bridge and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in a single trip. Light pressure due to its distance from main ramps is a consistent advantage.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes essentially the same playbook as Mack Bayou today — falling tide over oyster bars and grass edges, with reds, trout, and flounder as realistic targets and low pressure as the defining advantage. Work it as a natural extension of a Mack Bayou run, moving east along the 30-A shoreline to cover both spots in one long-run trip. The calm SSW winds today make the run and the fishing conditions about as good as you'll get in August, but the post-1 PM storm window demands a firm turnaround time — begin your run back well before noon to stay safe. Live shrimp or a slow-rolled soft plastic along the oyster structure at the mouth is the percentage play in slightly stained water under bright sun. The bay-wide bite report supports active reds and trout across the bay's protected bayous, and Hewett's light pressure makes it worth the run.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is limited basis to speak confidently about it. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou isn't worth a dedicated long run from the 331 Bridge, but if you're already out on the 30-A side fishing Mack and Hewett, it's a low-cost addition that could produce redfish or trout on the same falling-tide pattern. Keep expectations calibrated — there's less documented fishing history here than its neighbors, so treat it as exploratory water rather than a reliable producer. Poke the mouth and any visible oyster structure with a live shrimp or weedless soft plastic and move on if nothing develops quickly. Given the post-1 PM storm window and the long open-water run back, time management is especially important on a three-bayou western trip — budget Buck as a brief stop, not an extended session. Calm winds today are your best friend for making this kind of multi-stop run work safely.
